_rules: Every step here is transcribed from the IFRC 2020 guidelines. Nothing is written by an AI and nothing is written from memory.
The AI only SELECTS a card. It never edits, reorders or adds a step.
Before the demo a second team member must proof-read every card against the cited pages.
Subtype codes must stay in sync with core/pipeline/RuleTriageEngine.kt.

cards.title: Not breathing - start CPR
cards.source: IFRC 2020, Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (adolescent and adult)

steps.text: Ask a bystander to call emergency services now, or call yourself. Put the phone on speaker.
Begin chest compressions without delay. Push down on the centre of the chest, fast and regular, 100 to 120 compressions per minute.
Ask a bystander to bring a defibrillator as soon as possible. Follow its voice prompts and interrupt compressions as little as possible.
If you are able and willing, combine compressions and rescue breaths at a ratio of 30 compressions to 2 breaths.
If another first aid provider is present, swap every one to two minutes to prevent getting tired. Do not interrupt CPR during the swap.
Continue until told to pause by the defibrillator or a professional responder, or until the person coughs, opens their eyes, speaks, moves purposefully and breathes normally.
Check that they are breathing normally. If the breathing is gasping, irregular or absent, stop and start CPR instead.
Move them onto their side and tilt their head back to keep the airway open. This is the recovery position. A baby can be held in this position in your arms, with the head in a neutral position.
Call emergency medical services.
Monitor their breathing and level of response. If you can, try to establish why they are unresponsive.
If you suspect a spine injury, do not roll them. Keep the airway open with a head-tilt-chin-lift or jaw thrust only, and call emergency services.
Ask the person to press on their own wound with their hands. This lowers infection risk for both of you.
Help the person to lie down.
Call emergency medical services.
Apply direct pressure to the bleed. Use a bandage, cloth or plastic as a barrier between your hand and the blood. If blood soaks through, add a second dressing on top of the first and press harder.
If direct pressure is not working and the bleed is on an arm or leg, consider a tourniquet if one is available. If not, consider a haemostatic dressing and keep up the direct pressure.
Expect shock after significant bleeding. Keep them lying on their back and keep them warm, wrapping them in clothing if needed.
If there is an object embedded in the wound, press around it and try to stabilise it. Do not remove it.
If they become unresponsive, open the airway and check breathing.
Move nearby objects away so they cannot hurt themselves. Do not move the person unless they are in immediate danger.
Put soft padding, such as a cushion or a sweater, under their head. Remove eyeglasses and loosen tight clothing around the neck. Do not restrain them and do not put anything in their mouth.
Note the time the seizure starts and stops, and whether it happens again. Tell emergency services.
Call emergency services if they hurt themselves, if it is their first seizure, if the seizure lasts more than five minutes, or if they do not regain responsiveness afterwards.
Also call if the seizures repeat or differ from their usual ones, if they are pregnant or diabetic, if they have a high fever, if alcohol or drugs are involved, or whenever you are in doubt.
When the seizure is over, check their breathing and keep checking. Remove the padding if it could block their breathing.
If they are breathing normally, move them onto their side and keep the airway open. If breathing is abnormal, start CPR.
For a baby or child, also check their temperature. If they are too hot, remove excess clothing and let them have fresh, cool air.
Tell them to stop all physical activity. Help them rest in a cool place and remove excess clothing.
For severe heatstroke, start cooling immediately. Immerse them in cold water for around 15 minutes, or until their temperature is below 39 degrees Celsius.
If immersion is not possible, use any active cooling you have: a cool wet sheet, wetting them with cold water, ice packs on the neck and groin. Fanning increases the cooling.
Call emergency medical services.
For mild to moderate heat illness, cool them with whatever is available and give them water to drink. Sports drinks or cold tea may also help.
Keep monitoring their temperature and their level of response. Aim to bring the temperature below 39 degrees Celsius.
Seek medical advice if they do not improve quickly, if they are a baby, child or older adult, if they are losing more fluid than they take in, or if they pass very little dark urine.
Help the person keep the injury still.
Support the injury in a comfortable position so it cannot move. Keeping the limb raised may reduce swelling.
Apply ice or something cold for up to 20 minutes. Always wrap an ice pack in a cloth. Cooling longer than this can damage the skin.
Call emergency medical services if there is a lot of pain or swelling, or if the limb is in an abnormal position.
If it is an open fracture, your priority is to stop the bleeding first, then stabilise the limb.
Reassure the person and keep them comfortable.
Help the person sit down in a comfortable position and take their own medication if they have it.
Call emergency services immediately if you suspect a heart attack. Say that you suspect a heart attack so they prioritise the call. Ask a bystander to bring a defibrillator if possible.

Suggest they consider chewing a dose of acetylsalicylic acid if a heart attack is suspected. Do not give it if they are allergic to it, have a bleeding disorder, or have already taken the recommended dose.
Reassure the person and monitor their breathing and responsiveness.
If they become unresponsive with abnormal breathing, start CPR.
Cool the burn with clean running water for at least 10 minutes, ideally 20 minutes. Do not use ice-cold water and do not apply ice.
Call emergency medical services if the burn is large or deep, is near the face, mouth, throat or genitals, or was caused by chemicals, electricity or flames.
Remove clothing and jewellery on or near the burn, as long as they are not stuck to the skin.
After cooling, cover it with a dressing that keeps moisture in, follows the shape of the wound and does not stick.
If you have to move the person to medical care, cover the burn with a wet cloth or plastic cling wrap.
Leave any blisters intact and seek medical advice.
Reassure the person and monitor their responsiveness, breathing and temperature, especially for a child or an older adult.
Treat what you find in order of severity. Deal with breathing and circulation first, because those are critical to survival.
Call for help if needed.
Keep assessing and observing. Watch for any change in their condition.
Stay with them until professional medical care takes over.
If more than one person is hurt, call emergency services first to warn them it is a potentially critical situation, then call again once you have details.
With multiple casualties, quickly assess everyone before treating anyone, and treat the most life-threatening breathing and circulation problems first.
